title: Kolkata's Iconic Flurys Opens First North India Outlet in Gurugram Ahead of Centenary
excerpt: The 99-year-old tearoom brings its Park Street heritage to Galleria Market as it eyes a national footprint before its 2027 centenary.
body:
• Flurys, the 99-year-old Kolkata tearoom, has opened its first North India outlet at Galleria Market in Gurugram ahead of its centenary in 2027.
  • The menu preserves heritage classics like the chicken patty, milk loaf, and rum balls alongside newer items like a Nolen Gur Creme Brulee served in a traditional clay bhar.
  • Founded in 1927 by Swiss couple Joseph Flury and Quinto Cinzio Trinca on Park Street, the brand is now owned by the Apeejay Surrendra Group.
  • Flurys has grown to roughly 15 outlets in Mumbai, several in Chennai, and locations in Hyderabad, Bhubaneswar, and other cities.

Flurys, the tearoom and patisserie that has been a fixture of Kolkata's Park Street since 1927, has opened its first North India outlet at Galleria Market in Gurugram, bringing nearly a century of baking heritage to the national capital region.

The expansion, reported exclusively by NDTV Food, comes as the brand approaches its centenary in 2027. For Kolkata natives scattered across India and the world, the name Flurys carries a weight that transcends pastry — it is bound up with memories of leisurely breakfasts, birthday cakes, and the particular atmosphere of Park Street.

What the Gurugram Outlet Looks Like

The new outlet sits within Galleria Market's open-air setting, surrounded by European-style walkways and boutique stores. Inside, the space features soft pink accents, cozy seating, and neatly arranged display counters. Red labels on several items mark recipes that have been part of the Flurys menu since before the 1970s — the brand's true classics.

The signature bright pink signage, familiar to anyone who has walked past the Park Street original, is prominently displayed.

The Menu

NDTV Food's review highlights several standouts. The vegetable puff, often overlooked at other bakeries, was described as exceptional — with beautifully flaky pastry and a generously packed, well-seasoned filling. The chicken patty delivered clean flavors with plenty of tender chicken, while the mutton puff offered a richer, bolder alternative.

Among the bakery classics, the almond croissant had crisp, buttery layers filled with marzipan and finished with sliced almonds. The iconic milk loaf — soft, pillowy, and lightly sweet — lived up to its reputation as the kind of bread that disappears before it reaches the dining table.

One of the more inventive offerings was the Nolen Gur Creme Brulee, served in a traditional clay bhar. The smoky caramel notes of Bengali date palm jaggery blended with silky French custard, creating what the reviewer called a dessert that felt "both familiar and inventive."

The beverage menu spans cold coffee, iced chocolate, and the Flurys Viennese Coffee finished with a generous swirl of whipped cream.

A Century of History

Flurys was founded in 1927 by Swiss business partners Joseph Flury and Quinto Cinzio Trinca at 18 Park Street. The partnership dissolved in 1939 — Trinca opened a rival tearoom, Trincas, diagonally opposite — and in 1965, Flury sold the business to Jit Paul, who integrated it into the Apeejay Surrendra Group.

The brand remained a Kolkata institution for decades before beginning a broader expansion. By 2025, Flurys had grown to approximately 15 outlets in Mumbai, several in Chennai, and locations in Hyderabad, Bhubaneswar, Indore, Gangtok, and Darjeeling. The Gurugram outlet marks its first entry into North India.

What It Means

The Gurugram opening is significant beyond mere geography. As NDTV Food noted, "When a legacy brand arrives in Delhi NCR, people know that while they are entering a new store, within its four walls lies a rich history, culture, legacy and oodles of nostalgia."

For the Bengali diaspora, Flurys is not just a bakery — it is a sensory connection to home. Its national expansion suggests the brand is positioning itself as a heritage-driven alternative to international cafe chains, trading on authenticity and institutional memory rather than trend-chasing menus.

No pricing details were disclosed in the initial review. The Gurugram outlet is now open to the public.
